PETITION FOR PROBATE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Pat Morgan

PROPOSED PETITIONER — INFORMATION AND DECLARATION IN SUPPORT OF PETITION
I, Jordan Lee, am the person petitioning the California superior court to open a probate proceeding for the estate of Pat Morgan, who died on August 1, 2026 at Sacramento, California. My relationship to Pat Morgan is: adult child. I am petitioning for appointment of Jordan Lee as personal representative of Pat Morgan's estate. The character and estimated value of the property in the estate is: Real property and financial accounts with an estimated total value of $650,000. This declaration provides background information for use with an actual petition for probate, to be filed in California superior court under Probate Code Division 7, Part 2. This declaration is not itself a court filing, and signing it does not open probate, appoint Jordan Lee — or anyone else — as personal representative, or determine the value of Pat Morgan's estate or the identity of Pat Morgan's heirs or devisees for any purpose. Only a court order issued after the statutory petition, notice, and hearing process described in this document can open probate or appoint a personal representative, and only the subsequent issuance of Letters Testamentary or Letters of Administration gives that personal representative actual authority to act for the estate.

THIS PETITION INFORMATION SHEET DESCRIBES A COURT PROCEEDING, NOT AN AUTOMATIC TRANSFER
Opening a formal probate proceeding for Pat Morgan's estate under California law happens only through an actual proceeding in superior court under Probate Code Division 7 — a filed petition, notice to interested persons, and a court order — not through the act of preparing or signing this document. Probate Code § 8000(a) provides that at any time after a decedent’s death, any interested person may commence proceedings for administration of the estate by a petition to the court for an order determining the date and place of death and for either or both appointment of a personal representative and probate of the decedent’s will. Probate Code § 48(a) separately defines “interested person,” for this and other probate purposes, to include an heir, devisee, child, spouse, creditor, beneficiary, and any other person having a property right in or claim against the estate that may be affected by the proceeding, as well as any person having priority for appointment as personal representative, and a fiduciary representing an interested person.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "At any time after a decedent’s death, any interested person may commence proceedings for administration of the estate of the decedent by a petition to the court for an order determining the date and place of the decedent’s death and for either or both of the following: (1) Appointment of a personal representative. (2) Probate of the decedent’s will."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8000(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8000(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8000.)
  "Subject to subdivision (b), “interested person” includes any of the following: (1) An heir, devisee, child, spouse, creditor, beneficiary, and any other person having a property right in or claim against a trust estate or the estate of a decedent which may be affected by the proceeding. (2) Any person having priority for appointment as personal representative. (3) A fiduciary representing an interested person."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 48(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 48(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=48.)

This document is informational: it describes the statutory probate petition process for estates that do not qualify for, or are not using, California's separate small-estate procedures (Prob. Code §§ 13100-13210); it does not itself open probate, appoint a personal representative, or determine the value of any specific estate or the identity of any specific decedent's heirs — only a court order issued after the statutory petition, notice, and hearing process can do that. This clause cites two different statutory sections (§ 8000(a) and § 48(a)); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. § 48(b) further notes that the meaning of “interested person” as applied to particular persons can vary by the purpose and matter involved in a given proceeding; this clause does not attempt to resolve that variation for any specific case.

CALIFORNIA DOES NOT SET A GENERAL DEADLINE TO FILE A PROBATE PETITION — ONLY A NARROW 30-DAY RULE FOR A NAMED EXECUTOR
Probate Code § 8001 does not impose a general deadline, running from Pat Morgan's date of death, by which a petition to open probate must be filed. The only timing rule found in this part of the code is narrower: unless good cause for the delay is shown, a person named as executor in a will who fails to petition the court for administration of the estate within 30 days after that person has knowledge of the decedent's death and of being named as executor may be held to have waived the right to appointment as personal representative. That 30-day rule applies only to a person named as executor in a will; it does not set a deadline for heirs or other interested persons to petition, and it does not itself bar the estate from being probated — it addresses only whether that particular named executor may lose priority for appointment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Unless good cause for delay is shown, if a person named in a will as executor fails to petition the court for administration of the estate within 30 days after the person has knowledge of the death of the decedent and that the person is named as executor, the person may be held to have waived the right to appointment as personal representative."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8001 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8001 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8001.)

This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's formal probate process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 8001); no additional independent source was found for this.

WHAT THE PETITION MUST STATE
Probate Code § 8002(a) requires a petition for administration of Pat Morgan's estate to contain: the date and place of Pat Morgan's death; the street address and county of Pat Morgan's residence at the time of death; the name, age, address, and relation to Pat Morgan of each heir and devisee, so far as known to or reasonably ascertainable by the petitioner; the character and estimated value of the property in the estate; and the name of the person for whom appointment as personal representative is petitioned. If Pat Morgan left a will, § 8002(b) separately requires the petitioner to attach a photographic copy of the will (plus a typed copy, if it is holographic or otherwise has handwritten material provisions, and an English translation if it is in a foreign language), and to state in the petition whether the person named as executor in the will consents to act or waives the right to appointment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The petition shall contain all of the following information: (1) The date and place of the decedent’s death. (2) The street number, street, and city, or other address, and the county, of the decedent’s residence at the time of death. (3) The name, age, address, and relation to the decedent of each heir and devisee of the decedent, so far as known to or reasonably ascertainable by the petitioner. (4) The character and estimated value of the property in the estate. (5) The name of the person for whom appointment as personal representative is petitioned."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8002(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8002(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8002.)
  "If the decedent left a will: (1) The petitioner shall attach to the petition a photographic copy of the will. In the case of a holographic will or other will of which material provisions are handwritten, the petitioner shall also attach a typed copy of the will. (2) If the will is in a foreign language, the petitioner shall attach an English language translation. On admission of the will to probate, the court shall certify to a correct translation into English, and the certified translation shall be filed with the will. (3) The petition shall state whether the person named as executor in the will consents to act or waives the right to appointment."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8002(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8002(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8002.)

This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 8002(a) and § 8002(b)). NOTICE BEFORE THE HEARING, AND THE CREDITOR CLAIM-FILING PERIOD IT STARTS
At least 15 days before the hearing on a petition for administration of Pat Morgan's estate, Probate Code § 8110 requires the petitioner to deliver notice of the hearing to each heir of Pat Morgan, so far as known to or reasonably ascertainable by the petitioner, and to each devisee, executor, and alternate executor named in any will being offered for probate, regardless of whether that devise or appointment is purportedly revoked by a later instrument. The statutory notice form set out at Probate Code § 8100 also fixes the outer limit for a creditor or contingent creditor of Pat Morgan to file a claim: within the later of four months from the date letters are first issued to a general personal representative, or 60 days from the date a particular creditor is delivered notice under Probate Code § 9052.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "At least 15 days before the hearing of a petition for administration of a decedent’s estate, the petitioner shall deliver notice of the hearing pursuant to Section 1215 on all of the following persons: (a) Each heir of the decedent, so far as known to or reasonably ascertainable by the petitioner. (b) Each devisee, executor, and alternative executor named in any will being offered for probate, regardless of whether the devise or appointment is purportedly revoked in a subsequent instrument."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8110 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8110 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8110.)
  "IF YOU ARE A CREDITOR or a contingent creditor of the deceased, you must file your claim with the court and mail a copy to the personal representative appointed by the court within the later of either (1) four months from the date of first issuance of letters to a general personal representative, as defined in subdivision (b) of Section 58 of the California Probate Code, or (2) 60 days from the date of delivery of the notice to you under Section 9052 of the California Probate Code."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8100 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8100 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8100.)

WHO THE COURT MAY APPOINT AS ADMINISTRATOR WHEN THERE IS NO WILL, AND IN WHAT ORDER
If Pat Morgan died intestate (without a valid will), Probate Code § 8460(a) requires the court to appoint an administrator as personal representative, and § 8460(b) allows the court to appoint more than one person to serve in that role. Probate Code § 8461 fixes the order of priority among persons entitled to that appointment: (a) surviving spouse or domestic partner; (b) children; (c) grandchildren; (d) other issue; (e) parents; (f) brothers and sisters; (g) issue of brothers and sisters; (h) grandparents; (i) issue of grandparents; (j) children of a predeceased spouse or domestic partner; (k) other issue of a predeceased spouse or domestic partner; (l) other next of kin; (m) parents of a predeceased spouse or domestic partner; (n) issue of parents of a predeceased spouse or domestic partner; (o) a conservator or guardian of the estate acting in that capacity at Pat Morgan's death who has filed a first account and is not acting as conservator or guardian for anyone else; (p) the public administrator; (q) creditors; and (r) any other person.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) If the decedent dies intestate, the court shall appoint an administrator as personal representative. (b) The court may appoint one or more persons as administrator."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8460 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8460 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8460.)
  "Subject to the provisions of this article, a person in the following relation to the decedent is entitled to appointment as administrator in the following order of priority: (a) Surviving spouse or domestic partner as defined in Section 37. (b) Children. (c) Grandchildren. (d) Other issue. (e) Parents. (f) Brothers and sisters. (g) Issue of brothers and sisters. (h) Grandparents. (i) Issue of grandparents. (j) Children of a predeceased spouse or domestic partner. (k) Other issue of a predeceased spouse or domestic partner. (l) Other next of kin. (m) Parents of a predeceased spouse or domestic partner. (n) Issue of parents of a predeceased spouse or domestic partner. (o) Conservator or guardian of the estate acting in that capacity at the time of death who has filed a first account and is not acting as conservator or guardian for any other person. (p) Public administrator. (q) Creditors. (r) Any other person."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 8461 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 8461 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=8461.)

This clause cites two different statutory sections (§ 8460 and § 8461); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. Several conditioning provisions in the same article are not quoted here and are honestly disclosed rather than described: § 8462 limits a spouse's, domestic partner's, or relative's priority to situations where that person is entitled to succeed to all or part of the estate (directly, or through another deceased person's entitlement); § 8463 gives a surviving spouse who was living apart from the decedent at death, while a party to a separate maintenance, annulment, or dissolution action, priority next after brothers and sisters instead of the priority § 8461 would otherwise give a spouse; and § 8464 lets the court, in its discretion, appoint a guardian or conservator (or another qualified person) in place of someone otherwise entitled to appointment who is a minor or has their own conservator of the estate. A PERSONAL REPRESENTATIVE HAS NO AUTHORITY TO ACT UNTIL LETTERS ARE ISSUED
Probate Code § 8400(a) provides that a person has no power to administer Pat Morgan's estate until that person is appointed personal representative and the appointment becomes effective, and that the appointment becomes effective only when the person appointed is issued letters. § 8400(b) makes this true whether or not the person is named executor in Pat Morgan's will, with one narrow exception: a person named executor may, before the appointment is made or becomes effective, pay funeral expenses and take necessary measures for the maintenance and preservation of the estate. § 8400(c) requires the court's order appointing a personal representative to carry, in capital letters on its first page, the warning that the appointment is not effective until letters have issued. Before letters are issued, Probate Code § 8403(a) separately requires the personal representative to take and subscribe an oath to perform the duties of the office according to law; § 8403(b) provides that the oath constitutes acceptance of the office and must be attached to or endorsed on the letters.

  "(a) A person has no power to administer the estate until the person is appointed personal representative and the appointment becomes effective. Appointment of a personal representative becomes effective when the person appointed is issued letters. INDEPENDENT ADMINISTRATION UNDER THE IAEA, AND THE MATTERS THAT STILL REQUIRE COURT SUPERVISION EVEN THEN
Once appointed, a personal representative for Pat Morgan's estate does not automatically administer that estate under full court supervision for every act. Probate Code § 10450(a) lets a personal representative petition the court — either in the petition for appointment or in a separate petition filed later in the estate proceeding — for authority to administer the estate under the Independent Administration of Estates Act (IAEA), and § 10450(b) lets that petition request either full or limited IAEA authority. Even where full or limited IAEA authority is granted, Probate Code § 10501(a) still requires the personal representative to obtain court supervision, in the manner otherwise provided by the Probate Code, for specified matters — among them, allowance of the personal representative's or their attorney's compensation, settlement of accounts, and preliminary or final distributions and discharge; § 10501(b) requires court supervision for sale or exchange of real property, and certain other real-property transactions, whenever only limited (rather than full) IAEA authority has been granted. Separately, Probate Code § 10404 provides that a personal representative may not be granted IAEA authority at all if Pat Morgan's will provides that the estate shall not be administered under the Act.

  "(a) To obtain authority to administer the estate under this part, the personal representative shall petition the court for that authority either in the petition for appointment of the personal representative or in a separate petition filed in the estate proceedings. (b) The petition may request either of the following: (1) Full authority to administer the estate under this part. (2) Limited authority to administer the estate under this part."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 10450 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 10450 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=10450.)
  "Notwithstanding any other provision of this part, whether the personal representative has been granted full authority or limited authority, a personal representative who has obtained authority to administer the estate under this part is required to obtain court supervision, in the manner provided in this code, for any of the following actions: (1) Allowance of the personal representative’s compensation. (2) Allowance of compensation of the attorney for the personal representative. (3) Settlement of accounts. (4) Subject to Section 10520, preliminary and final distributions and discharge."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 10501(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 10501(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=10501.)
  "The personal representative may not be granted authority to administer the estate under this part if the decedent’s will provides that the estate shall not be administered under this part."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 10404 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 10404 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=10404.)

This clause cites three different statutory sections (§ 10450, § 10501, and § 10404); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. § 10501(a) lists ten specific categories of action requiring court supervision even under full IAEA authority, and § 10501(b) lists four further categories requiring it under limited authority alone; this clause summarizes rather than reproduces every listed category, and § 10501(c) sets out a narrow exception to some of those categories (for certain sole-beneficiary or fully-consented transactions after the creditor-claim period has run) that this clause does not otherwise describe. expectedJSON.body: Once appointed, a personal representative for Pat Morgan's estate does not automatically administer that estate under full court supervision for every act. Probate Code § 10450(a) lets a personal representative petition the court — either in the petition for appointment or in a separate petition filed later in the estate proceeding — for authority to administer the estate under the Independent Administration of Estates Act (IAEA), and § 10450(b) lets that petition request either full or limited IAEA authority. Even where full or limited IAEA authority is granted, Probate Code § 10501(a) still requires the personal representative to obtain court supervision, in the manner otherwise provided by the Probate Code, for specified matters — among them, allowance of the personal representative's or their attorney's compensation, settlement of accounts, and preliminary or final distributions and discharge; § 10501(b) requires court supervision for sale or exchange of real property, and certain other real-property transactions, whenever only limited (rather than full) IAEA authority has been granted. Separately, Probate Code § 10404 provides that a personal representative may not be granted IAEA authority at all if Pat Morgan's will provides that the estate shall not be administered under the Act.

(b) The petition may request either of the following: (1) Full authority to administer the estate under this part. (2) Limited authority to administer the estate under this part.

(2) Allowance of compensation of the attorney for the personal representative. (3) Settlement of accounts. (4) Subject to Section 10520, preliminary and final distributions and discharge.
